paragraphs.heading: A secret network
paragraphs.text: The Underground Railroad was an organised web of hidden routes and safe houses that helped people escaping slavery in the United States reach the abolitionist North and Eastern Canada. Enslaved people had run away as early as the 1500s, often with no help at all. But from the 1780s, abolitionist societies in the North began to build a network of safe houses, and it kept growing until Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863.

paragraphs.heading: Who made it work
paragraphs.text: Most of the work was done by African Americans, both free and enslaved, with help from abolitionists and others who sided with the people escaping. Those who fled were called passengers and those who helped them were called conductors. The route started at the very place where a person was enslaved. Escapees mostly aimed for free states or for Canada.

paragraphs.heading: Many roads to freedom
paragraphs.text: Routes followed both natural and built paths: rivers, canals, bays, the Atlantic coast, ferries, roads and trails. Places near ports, free territory and international borders led to many escapes. Not every route ran north; some led to Mexico, which had abolished slavery, and to Caribbean islands outside the slave trade. Many people escaped by sea, among them Ona Judge, whom President George Washington had held in slavery.

paragraphs.heading: A name that began as a joke
paragraphs.text: Scott Shane traced the earliest printed use of the name to a column of August 10, 1842, written by Thomas Smallwood, a Black abolitionist based in Washington, D.C. Smallwood said he was quoting a Baltimore constable, John Zell, who, exasperated by how many people were escaping, said they must be travelling by steam balloon or underground rail-road. Both were new and rather fanciful technologies at the time. Smallwood meant it to mock the enslavers' surprise, but the joke stuck, and other abolitionists soon used it for the whole effort.

paragraphs.heading: Laws that fed the network
paragraphs.text: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 made officials in free states help slaveholders recapture people who had fled, though some states refused. Because the law made it easier to seize African Americans and return them to slavery, it pushed abolitionists to help, and anti-slavery societies and the Underground Railroad grew. The Compromise of 1850 brought a harsher Fugitive Slave Law that took away a suspect's right to defend themselves in court. Since so little paperwork was needed to claim someone was a fugitive, slave catchers also kidnapped free Black people, especially children, and sold them into slavery.

paragraphs.heading: How many escaped
paragraphs.text: One estimate puts the number who had escaped through the network by 1850 at about 100,000. J. Blaine Hudson, a former professor of Pan-African studies, put the figure at 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War. Many who rode the Underground Railroad saw Canada as their final stop, and somewhere between 30,000 and 40,000 settled there, half of them between 1850 and 1860. Others made new homes in the free states of the North.
